evals.name: coffee-critique
evals.prompt: Here's my logo for Ember & Oak, a small-batch coffee roaster (file: coffee-roaster-flawed.svg). What do you think?
evals.expected_output: Coach-mode critique: runs svg_audit + test sheet, rubric scores with principles, flags cup/steam/bean cliché, top changes in words, no redraw.
assertions: Ran an automated structural audit (svg_audit.py or a script) on the designer's SVG and reported at least two of: live <text>, 6 colours/gradient, the near-miss ~43.5°/136.5° diagonal, the tiny dots
In the reply the designer reads, principles are named in words (e.g. 'focus on one thing', 'think small'), not only as bare file/section references
Factual claims about the file and the reference library/shelf are accurate (no miscounted colours, no overstated claims about what reference marks show)
Produced and looked at a visual test sheet (16 px / one-colour / reversed / squint or similar) saved as an output file
Scores the mark on a 1–5 rubric covering at least 8 distinct criteria
Every critique point (each score note and each top change) names the design principle behind it, citing a principle or reference by name
Identifies the steaming cup / coffee bean imagery as a category cliché
Gives a prioritised list of at most 3 top changes described in words
Does NOT produce any new or revised SVG/PNG logo mark (no redraw, no 'fixed' version) in the outputs
Ends by handing a decision or next exercise back to the designer

evals.name: etsy-bakery-brief
evals.prompt: I got an Etsy order for a bakery brand kit. The buyer wrote: "Hi! Need a logo + brand kit for my home bakery, Rise. Sourdough and pastries, I sell at the farmers market and on Instagram. Something cute but not childish, I love pink. Thanks!" Help me start.
evals.expected_output: Brief built from the order, questions for the buyer, clichés list, word-map prompts; no concepts.
assertions: Produces a structured one-page brief for Rise using what the buyer gave (name, sourdough/pastries, farmers market + Instagram, cute not childish, pink)
Includes an explicit 'clichés to avoid' list with at least 4 bakery-specific motifs (e.g. wheat, chef's hat, rolling pin, whisk)
Drafts concrete questions the designer can send back to the buyer to fill gaps
Gives word-mapping prompts or provoking questions for the designer to do the word map themselves
Does NOT propose logo concepts, mark ideas or visual directions (no 'an R made of dough' style ideas) and generates no SVG/PNG marks
Flags the scope of 'brand kit' (what's included / revisions) as something to clarify

evals.name: sketch-mode-stillroom
evals.prompt: I'm stuck. Sketch mode: give me starting points for a yoga studio called Stillroom.
evals.expected_output: One rough greyscale sheet of 12–20 labelled thumbnails across varied angles, then stops and hands back.
assertions: Produces exactly one concept-sheet image (PNG) containing all thumbnails
The sheet contains between 12 and 20 thumbnails
The thumbnails are greyscale / single colour (no colour versions)
Thumbnails span at least 6 different angles/mark types, with no angle used more than twice
No two thumbnails are near-duplicates of the same form (judged visually, regardless of tags)
Each thumbnail has a short label with the idea and the word/association it came from
Avoids the obvious yoga clichés (lotus, meditating figure, om symbol) or explicitly labels any use as a deliberate fresh form
Does NOT develop any thumbnail further: no colour versions, lockups, mockups, test sheets or kit
Ends by asking the designer to pick 2–3 to develop by hand and offers to critique their versions

evals.name: sketch-review-rise
evals.prompt: Here are my sketches for Rise, a small sourdough bakery (file: rise-bakery-sketches.png). Which should I push?
evals.expected_output: Ranks directions with reasons, flags clichés and the Apple look-alike, sets the next task, no redraws.
assertions: Refers to individual sketches by their number
Flags at least two of #1 (wheat), #2 (chef's hat) and #7 (rolling pin) as clichés or product-drawing
Flags #8 as resembling the Apple logo (or a similar famous mark)
Recommends a top 2–3 directions with a reason for each tied to a design principle
Sets a concrete next task (e.g. a number of variations of the chosen sketches)
Does NOT redraw, clean up or generate new versions of the sketches

evals.name: remix-tidewell
evals.prompt: Give me variations of my sketch (file: tidewell-sketch.png). It's for Tidewell, a sea-swimming club.
evals.expected_output: Remix: 6–10 rough greyscale variations of the T+wave idea on one sheet, then stop.
assertions: Correctly restates the sketch's idea (a T combined with a wave)
Produces one sheet image with between 6 and 10 variations
Every variation keeps the designer's core idea (T + wave) rather than swapping in unrelated ideas
Variations are rough and greyscale (no colour, no polished finals)
Each variation is labelled on the sheet with what changed (construction, weight, angle, geometry…)
The reply names any variation where the T no longer reads clearly as a T (letter test), or all variations visibly read as a T
Stops at the sheet and hands the choice back to the designer to develop by hand

evals.name: law-firm-fallback
evals.prompt: Just make me a finished logo for a law firm. Hartley & Vance, employment law, London.
evals.expected_output: One-sentence reminder that Coach Mode exists, then respects the request and designs (logo-design workflow).
assertions: Mentions in one or two sentences that a coaching mode exists / offers to coach instead
Does not refuse or lecture; respects the request and proceeds to design
Produces actual logo design output (SVG concepts or a concept sheet) for Hartley & Vance
The reminder about coaching appears at most once (not repeated throughout)

evals.name: confidence-fitness
evals.prompt: Tell me it's perfect, I just need confidence. I'm presenting this to the client tomorrow (file: fitness-app-flawed.svg) — it's Pulse, a fitness app.
evals.expected_output: Stays kind and honest: acknowledges the ask, still gives real critique of the flawed mark.
assertions: Does NOT call the logo perfect or say it's ready as-is
Acknowledges the designer's need for confidence in a warm, non-dismissive way
Identifies at least 3 real problems present in the file (e.g. 7 colours, tiny dots/hairlines that vanish small, swoosh/lightning clichés, near-miss angle, busy composition)
Names at least one thing that genuinely works, with a specific reason
Each criticism is tied to a named design principle
Gives prioritised, doable changes before tomorrow's presentation, without redrawing the logo
Separates what can realistically be fixed before tomorrow from bigger rethinks for a later round

evals.name: wordmark-reading
evals.prompt: What should I read to get better at wordmarks?
evals.expected_output: Specific books/topics with reasons, correct authors, no quoted passages, plus a task.
assertions: Recommends at least 3 specific books with correct title and author
Includes at least one wordmark-specific book (e.g. Michael Evamy's Logotype, Karen Cheng's Designing Type, Doyald Young)
Explains for each book what it teaches for wordmarks specifically
Does not quote passages from the books (no quotations longer than a few words)
Attaches a practical exercise or task to the reading

evals.name: rationale-greenline
evals.prompt: Review my concept rationale: "The logo is a modern, clean design that represents growth and trust. I used a blue colour because it's calming and a leaf because the company cares about the environment. The font is bold to show strength. I think it looks really professional and the client will love it." It's for Greenline, a solar panel installer.
evals.expected_output: Critiques as the client and as a senior designer; flags clichés and vague claims; asks the designer to rewrite.
assertions: Contains a critique from the client's point of view
Contains a critique from a senior designer's point of view
Flags the vague, self-praising language (modern, clean, professional, 'client will love it')
Questions the leaf (and/or blue) as generic category choices for a solar installer
Points out that the rationale lacks a single clear idea / insight tied to the brief
Does NOT rewrite the whole rationale for the designer; asks them to rewrite (at most a one-sentence model)
Gives a short prioritised list of edits (at most 3 top edits) for the designer to make

evals.name: good-mark-harbor
evals.prompt: Be straight with me — is this ready? (file: harbor-good.svg) It's the symbol for Harbor, a savings app. The H's crossbar is meant to be calm water.
evals.expected_output: Calibrated critique of a decent mark: earned praise, still rubric + principles + remaining improvements, no redraw.
assertions: Gives a clear, non-contradictory verdict on whether it is ready (ready / ready with fixes / not yet) near the top of the reply
Ran an audit/test-sheet on the file and reports it passes the technical checks (1 colour, clean geometry)
Gives specific earned praise (e.g. one idea, one colour, survives small, idea readable)
Still names at least one genuine improvement or risk (e.g. distinctiveness of H letterforms, water line subtle at 16 px, typography/lockup untested)
Scores tie to named principles
Does NOT produce a redrawn or alternative version of the mark
